stories.title: The Greeks against the Persian Empire
stories.happened: The largest state of the world at that time twice marched against the scattered Greek cities. At Marathon, the Athenians with a small force of allies met a Persian landing. Ten years later, dozens of cities that were often at odds with one another formed an alliance and united their fleets.
stories.outcome: At Marathon (490 BC) and in the naval battle off Salamis (480 BC) the Greeks won. The Persian campaign against Greece failed. Ancient sources exaggerate the size of the armies, but historians do not dispute the outcome.
stories.lesson: The small can stand against the great when they set aside their quarrels and act together.

stories.title: The Netherlands: eighty years
stories.happened: The provinces of the Netherlands rose against the rule of the Spanish king: taxes, executions, religious persecution, suppression of liberties. Several times the revolt was on the brink of defeat. Besieged Leiden was saved by breaching the dikes: the water carried the rebels' ships up to the city walls.
stories.outcome: The northern provinces united (the Union of Utrecht, 1579) and held out. The struggle went on, with interruptions, for 80 years. In 1648, under the Peace of Münster, Spain recognised the independence of the Republic of the United Provinces.
stories.lesson: Resistance is a long distance. The one who does not give up over decades wins.

stories.title: Finland: the Winter War
stories.happened: On 30 November 1939 the USSR attacked Finland, which had many times fewer people and weapons. The Finns defended every line, fought in small ski units in the forests and inflicted heavy losses on the attacker.
stories.outcome: Under the Treaty of Moscow, signed on 12 March 1940, Finland ceded about a tenth of its territory, including Vyborg, and resettled more than 400,000 people from there. But the country was not occupied and kept its independence and its system of government.
stories.lesson: Determined resistance from the first days preserved the state, even at the cost of heavy losses.

stories.title: The Polish Underground State
stories.happened: In 1939 Poland was occupied by Germany and the USSR. Poles did not recognise the occupation: a government in exile operated abroad, and inside the country there was an underground administration, courts, press, secret schools and universities, and the Home Army, one of the largest underground armies in Europe.
stories.outcome: The underground preserved state structures and education under terror. The Warsaw Uprising of 1944 was brutally crushed, and after the war the country came under a regime imposed by the USSR. Poland regained full freedom only in 1989.
stories.lesson: A state can be preserved even when its territory is seized: in its people, its education, its organisation.

stories.title: Denmark: a rescue within weeks
stories.happened: The occupation authorities were preparing a round-up of Denmark's Jews. Word of it got out, and ordinary people — neighbours, fishermen, doctors, students — over a few weeks hid families and ferried them by boat across the strait to neutral Sweden.
stories.outcome: About 7,200 of the country's roughly 7,500 Jews escaped, along with about 700 of their relatives. About 470 people were deported to Theresienstadt; several dozen died, and the rest lived to see liberation — partly because the Danish authorities kept demanding information about them.
stories.lesson: The civic courage of many ordinary people is stronger than an occupier's order.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Rescue in Denmark

stories.title: The Baltic states: half a century of non-recognition
stories.happened: In 1940 the USSR occupied Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. There were mass deportations in 1941 and 1949. After the war the armed resistance of the "Forest Brothers" continued in the forests for years. The United States and many other states never recognised the annexation.
stories.outcome: The memory and legal continuity of the states were kept alive for decades. In 1990–1991 all three countries restored their independence as a continuation of the states that had existed before the occupation.
stories.lesson: Occupation does not become lawful with time. Non-recognition and memory keep the door to freedom open.

sources.title: Britannica: Estonia — Soviet occupation and independence

stories.title: The Baltic Way and the Vilnius TV Tower
stories.happened: On 23 August 1989 about two million people joined hands in a human chain more than 600 kilometres long, from Vilnius through Riga to Tallinn. In January 1991 Soviet troops stormed the TV tower in Vilnius; unarmed people stood around it.
stories.outcome: On 13 January 1991, 14 people were killed and hundreds were wounded. But the Lithuanians did not disperse, and the authorities could not crush the independence restored on 11 March 1990. In the same year, 1991, the world recognised it.
stories.lesson: Peaceful, mass and confident unity is also a weapon that aggressors fear.

sources.title: Литовська національна комісія ЮНЕСКО: Балтійський шлях у реєстрі «Пам'ять світу» (Lithuanian National Commission for UNESCO: The Baltic Way in the Memory of the World Register)

stories.title: The Revolution on Granite and 1991
stories.happened: In October 1990 students in Kyiv declared a hunger strike in tents on the square. Thousands of people across Ukraine supported them. Two weeks later the Verkhovna Rada made concessions, and the head of government resigned.
stories.outcome: On 24 August 1991 the Verkhovna Rada adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine. On 1 December 1991, in a referendum, it was supported by more than 90 per cent of participants, with a turnout of more than 84 per cent.
stories.lesson: Peaceful, persistent pressure from society can change the course of history.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies): Revolution on Granite

Верховна Рада України: Постанова «Про проголошення незалежності України» з текстом Акта (Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine: Resolution "On the Declaration of Independence of Ukraine" with the text of the Act)

stories.title: The defence of Kyiv
stories.happened: On 24 February 2022 Russia launched its full-scale invasion and advanced on Kyiv from several directions, counting on taking the capital within a few days. It was met by the army, territorial defence, volunteers and local communities: Hostomel, Irpin, Moshchun, Brovary.
stories.outcome: At the end of March the enemy withdrew. In early April the Kyiv region was liberated. In Bucha and other towns, the killings of civilians during the occupation came to light.
stories.lesson: The unity of the army and communities thwarted the plan for a quick seizure.

sources.title: RUSI: Preliminary Lessons in Conventional Warfighting from Russia's Invasion of Ukraine (2022)
Управління ООН з прав людини (OHCHR): доповіді щодо Київської області (UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR): reports on the Kyiv region)

stories.title: Kherson: resistance under occupation
stories.happened: In early March 2022 Kherson was occupied. Residents came out to peaceful rallies with flags, spread the signs of the Yellow Ribbon movement and helped Ukrainian forces. For this, people were detained and tortured.
stories.outcome: On 11 November 2022 Kherson was liberated. Investigators and the UN Commission documented places of detention where people had been tortured.
stories.lesson: Even under occupation, resistance continues, and it brings liberation closer.

sources.title: Незалежна міжнародна комісія ООН з розслідування щодо України: доповіді 2023 року (UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine: 2023 reports)

stories.title: Batu's invasion and the fall of Kyiv
stories.happened: The Mongol army advanced on the lands of Rus. For years the princes had feuded among themselves and did not unite. Kyiv changed hands several times: Prince Mykhailo fled to Hungary, and Danylo of Halych left his voivode Dmytro in the city. It was he who led the defence.
stories.outcome: At the end of 1240, after a siege, Kyiv was taken and destroyed. The lands of Rus fell into dependence on the Horde for centuries.
stories.lesson: Discord in the face of a common threat costs more than any dispute.

stories.title: Konotop and the Ruin
stories.happened: In 1659 Hetman Ivan Vyhovsky, together with his Crimean allies, routed a large Muscovite army at Konotop. But within the Hetmanate itself the officer elite was divided by feuds, and some of the Cossacks rose against the hetman.
stories.outcome: That same year Vyhovsky gave up the mace. The Ruin began — decades of internecine strife, when hetmans sought support from different neighbours. In 1667, by the Andrusovo Truce, Ukraine was divided along the Dnipro between the Tsardom of Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
stories.lesson: Victory on the battlefield does not hold without unity at home.

stories.title: Baturyn
stories.happened: In 1708 Hetman Ivan Mazepa came out against Peter I. The tsar's army under Menshikov approached the hetman's capital, Baturyn. The town was taken after a defence, according to tradition, through treachery.
stories.outcome: Baturyn was burned, and its defenders and residents, including women and children, were killed — by various estimates, thousands of people died. Archaeological excavations confirm the mass killing. The massacre was used to intimidate the whole Hetmanate.
stories.lesson: The aggressor punishes civilians to break the will of others. Intimidation is its weapon.

sources.title: Канадський інститут українських студій: Батуринський проєкт (розкопки з університетом «Чернігівський колегіум») (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies: Baturyn Project, excavations with the Chernihiv Collegium University)

stories.title: The Ukrainian Revolution
stories.happened: After the fall of the empire, Ukraine proclaimed its own state: on 22 January 1918 the Fourth Universal of the Central Rada declared independence. But the leaders quarrelled, the regular army was weak, and internal conflicts and the rule of warlord otamans drained much of its strength.
stories.outcome: The Ukrainian state did not survive the war with the Bolsheviks and other adversaries. In 1921 the Treaty of Riga fixed the division of Ukrainian lands between Poland and the Soviet republics. Then came terror, the shooting of the intelligentsia and the Holodomor of 1932–1933, recognised in Ukraine as genocide.
stories.lesson: Without a strong army and unity, a state is lost, and millions pay the price.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Ukrainian National Republic
Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Riga, Peace Treaty of
Закон України «Про Голодомор 1932–1933 років в Україні» (Law of Ukraine "On the Holodomor of 1932–1933 in Ukraine")

stories.title: Munich: peace at the price of someone else's land
stories.happened: In September 1938 Great Britain and France, together with Italy, agreed in Munich that Germany could take the border regions of Czechoslovakia. Czechoslovakia itself was not invited to the talks. The British Prime Minister promised "peace for our time".
stories.outcome: Half a year later, in March 1939, Germany occupied the rest of the Czech lands. In September of the same year the Second World War began.
stories.lesson: Concessions to an aggressor do not bring peace — they only encourage it to go further.

stories.title: Budapest 1956, Prague 1968
stories.happened: In 1956 Hungarians rose against the regime imposed by the USSR. In 1968 Czechoslovakia attempted peaceful reforms — the Prague Spring. In 1956 the Hungarians hoped for help from the West; in 1968 the Czechs and Slovaks put up no armed resistance.
stories.outcome: Soviet tanks crushed the Hungarian uprising; thousands of people were killed, and about 200,000 fled the country. In 1968 troops of the USSR and four other Warsaw Pact countries occupied Czechoslovakia. The world did not intervene. These countries regained their freedom only in 1989.
stories.lesson: Resistance alone, without the support of friends, comes at a high price. Alliances must be built in advance.

stories.title: The Budapest Memorandum
stories.happened: After 1991 Ukraine was left with one of the largest nuclear arsenals in the world. On 5 December 1994 the United States, Great Britain and Russia signed a memorandum: Ukraine renounces nuclear weapons, and they undertake to respect its independence and borders and to refrain from the threat of force.
stories.outcome: Ukraine removed all nuclear warheads by 1996. In 2014 Russia, one of the signatories, seized Crimea and started the war in Donbas. The English original uses "assurances", not guarantees with an obligation to defend; the official Ukrainian translation uses the word "guarantees".
stories.lesson: Paper without strength does not protect. Security rests on one's own defence and reliable alliances.

sources.title: ООН: Меморандум про гарантії безпеки (документ A/49/765) (United Nations: Memorandum on Security Assurances, document A/49/765)

stories.title: Crimea under occupation
stories.happened: At the end of February 2014 Russian soldiers without insignia began seizing Crimea. In resolution 68/262 the UN General Assembly affirmed its commitment to the territorial integrity of Ukraine and called for non-recognition of any change in the status of Crimea.
stories.outcome: UN reports record in occupied Crimea the forced imposition of citizenship, persecution of Crimean Tatars and other dissenters, the ban on the Mejlis, detentions and enforced disappearances.
stories.lesson: Occupation brings not peace but repression. Refusing to recognise the occupation is also resistance.

sources.title: Генеральна Асамблея ООН: резолюція 68/262 (UN General Assembly: resolution 68/262)
Управління ООН з прав людини: доповіді щодо Криму (UN Human Rights Office: reports on Crimea)

stories.title: What occupation brings
stories.happened: In the lands seized after 24 February 2022, people found themselves under the rule of the occupiers: filtration, searches, detention of those who had served, volunteered or simply refused to submit.
stories.outcome: The UN Commission has established war crimes: torture, including torture resulting in death, sexual violence, unlawful deportation of children. In 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants, including for the President of Russia, for the deportation of Ukrainian children.
stories.lesson: Occupation does not bring peace: it is not the end of the war but a war against people.

sources.title: Незалежна міжнародна комісія ООН з розслідування щодо України (UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine)
Міжнародний кримінальний суд: ордери на арешт, 17 березня 2023 року (International Criminal Court: arrest warrants, 17 March 2023)

stories.title: Uprisings in the Gulag camps
stories.happened: In the Soviet special camps of Norilsk (1953) and Kengir (1954), prisoners — many of them Ukrainians — refused to work, elected their own committees and demanded humane conditions and a review of their cases.
stories.outcome: The uprisings were crushed — in Norilsk by gunfire, in Kengir by tanks; people were killed. But they showed that terror had not broken people, and they contributed to the easing of the camp regime and the release of many prisoners.
stories.lesson: Resistance is possible even where everything seems broken.

stories.title: The Ukrainian Helsinki Group and Vasyl Stus
stories.happened: On 9 November 1976 the Ukrainian Public Group to Promote the Implementation of the Helsinki Accords was founded in Kyiv. Its members openly collected evidence of violations of human and national rights. The poet Vasyl Stus joined it in 1979.
stories.outcome: Most of its members were sentenced to labour camps and exile; some died. Vasyl Stus died in a camp in 1985. Many of those who survived became co-founders of independent Ukraine: Levko Lukianenko wrote the text of the Act of Declaration of Independence.
stories.lesson: A word of truth is also resistance. Its price is high, but it outlives its tormentors.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Ukrainian Helsinki Group

stories.title: What follows from this
stories.happened: Resistance is a long distance. The Netherlands fought for 80 years, the Baltic states waited half a century, and both times those who did not give up won.
stories.outcome: Unity matters more than ideal conditions: Kyiv in 1240 and the Ruin show the price of discord, Salamis and the Baltic Way the strength of unity. Concessions to an aggressor do not bring peace: Munich, the Budapest Memorandum. Occupation brings not calm but repression: Baturyn, Crimea, 2022.
stories.lesson: Everyone has a role: not only the military, but also doctors, teachers, volunteers, neighbours, and those who speak the truth.
